title: The hidden life (CCC 531–534)
hook: most of Jesus's life was ordinary work in Nazareth

segments.voice: Yesterday, born of the Virgin: Mary's practical question, and her yes. Your line was by the holy spirit. Today, the years nobody wrote down.

"Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?" That's the hometown crowd in Mark's Gospel, and they aren't impressed. Jesus has come back to his own country, teaching in the synagogue, and the people who watched him grow up can't square it. They know his mother. They know his brothers by name. They know him as the carpenter. Their question is accidentally a window. Before the crowds and the miracles, there were years so ordinary that the neighbors remembered him mostly as a tradesman. The Catechism has a name for those years.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `THE NEIGHBORS CAN'T SQUARE IT.` → `YEARS NOBODY WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The hidden life. For the greater part of his life, the Catechism says, Jesus shared the condition of the vast majority of people: a daily life without evident greatness, manual work, the religious life of his people, life in a community. The Gospels are nearly silent about them. The one event that breaks the silence, the Catechism says, is the finding in the temple. When Jesus was twelve, Luke tells, his family went up to Jerusalem for the feast, and on the way home his parents realized he wasn't with them. After three days they found him in the temple, among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Then a line closes the door on the hidden years again. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Luke adds one more sentence: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." Back to the workshop, the family table, the synagogue on the sabbath. The Catechism sees in his obedience to Mary and Joseph a picture of his obedience to the Father. And because of Nazareth, it says, anyone can share in Jesus's life through the most ordinary events of their own day. It quotes Pope Paul the Sixth, speaking at Nazareth, who called it a school: a lesson in silence, in family life, in work. So the plain parts of a life aren't a waiting room before the real thing starts. In Catholic teaching, God made flesh spent most of his years on them.
screen: `THE GREATER PART: PLAIN DAYS.` · `THE GOSPELS ARE NEARLY SILENT.` · `HE WENT DOWN TO NAZARETH.` · `A SCHOOL OF SILENCE, FAMILY, WORK.` · then, large: `AND WAS SUBJECT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the plainest job waiting for you today, dishes, emails, a diaper, a shift, a form, and don't try to make it meaningful. Just see yourself doing it carefully, as if the person it serves were in the room, and notice your hands and the pace you'd like to go at. If you pray, offer that one task to God before you start; if you don't, simply choose the person you're doing it for.
The hidden life. Jesus's quiet years in Nazareth, with almost nothing written down. Today's word.
Your line: nazareth counts. The neighbors saw a carpenter, and that was part of it too. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Catholics honor the hidden life at Nazareth on the feast of the Holy Family and in the rosary's joyful mysteries, which end with the finding of Jesus in the temple.

chat.says: What was Jesus doing before he started preaching? Anything important?
options: Ordinary life in Nazareth: work, family, prayer. The Catechism says those plain years are a school for ours.
Nothing worth knowing: the Catechism says those years don't matter, only his public ministry.
He spent them studying in the Jerusalem temple, which is why the teachers there were amazed.
chat.meaning: For most of his life Jesus shared ordinary days: work, family, the religious life of his people. The Catechism says anyone can share in his life through ordinary events.

Nazareth.meaning: the town where Jesus grew up

synagogue.meaning: a Jewish house of prayer and study

Paul the Sixth.meaning: a pope who spoke at Nazareth, quoted in the Catechism

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Mark 6:3 (first clause), Luke 2:51 and Luke 2:52.
'The greater part of his life' and 'the vast majority' are CCC 531's own words (paraphrased); 'the one event that breaks that silence' paraphrases CCC 534 ('the only event'). Confirm.
Age twelve and 'after three days' are from Luke 2:42, 46.
Paul VI's Nazareth address (lessons of silence, family life, work) paraphrased from CCC 533; the date is left out under the claims rule.
'The God who took flesh spent most of that flesh's time on them' restates CCC 531 in plain words; Keeper may prefer a softer line.
